name: GAMBIT
expansion: Game-Theoretic Analysis of Model Behavior & Interactions

intro.problem: A two-network background method needs its input features split between the two networks, and that split is usually chosen by hand even though features interact and the choice directly shapes how well the estimate closes.
intro.value: A principled, data-driven partition would make the background estimate more defensible and would reveal which features actually drive closure, rather than leaving that to intuition.
intro.approach: We cast feature assignment as a game: a cooperative stage measures each feature's contribution against permutation nulls, an adversarial stage lets the two networks compete for features with closure as the referee, and every result is re-measured on seeds disjoint from the selection.
intro.goals: The outcome is an end-to-end selection pipeline, partitions validated on held-out seeds, and an honest accounting of what improved closure costs in discrimination.

questions: Which features actually drive background closure?
Does letting the networks compete for features produce a better partition than a hand-built one?
What does improved closure cost in discrimination, and when is that trade worth making?

timeline.label: Idea set: the two networks compete for input features, with background-estimate closure as the shared stake
Program fixed: plain baseline first, then one adversarial game and one cooperative game
Cooperative scoring rebuilt so selection and evaluation no longer share the same noise
First end-to-end run: cooperative feature selection fed into the adversarial game on one detector region
Review deck covering all builds; project officially named GAMBIT
Collect closure-term statistics on the barrel region first
Re-run the games on new data with closure as the referee
Run the full pipeline end to end on the endcap region
